description: Finding network weaknesses via penetration testing and protecting with access control and firewalls.
content_html:
Why Network Security Matters

Every connected device is a potential target. A school network holds thousands of student and staff records. A hospital network carries patient data. A retail network processes payment details. network security is the combination of measures that protect these systems. A single unguarded entry point can expose an entire organisation’s data — which is why securing networks requires both identifying vulnerabilities before attackers do, and putting protections in place to prevent or limit damage if an attack occurs.

Network security thinking divides into two clear stages: identification (finding weaknesses) and protection (preventing or containing attacks). Both are equally important. A network that is well protected but never tested for new vulnerabilities will eventually be exploited through an overlooked weakness.

Identifying Vulnerabilities: Penetration Testing

penetration testing (often called “pen testing”) is the practice of deliberately attempting to break into a network or system — with the organisation’s knowledge and permission — to find security weaknesses. The goal is to discover vulnerabilities before a genuine attacker does, so they can be fixed. Penetration testers produce a detailed report of every weakness found, how it was exploited, and how to remediate it.

Penetration tests can target network infrastructure (routers, switches, firewalls), individual devices on the network, or the software running on those devices. A thorough pen test may include trying to intercept unencrypted network traffic, testing whether wireless access points accept weak passwords, or attempting to connect unauthorised devices to the network.

Key Fact

Penetration testing is only legal and ethical if the organisation explicitly authorises it in writing. The same techniques used in a pen test — scanning for open ports, attempting to bypass authentication, intercepting traffic — would be crimes under the Computer Misuse Act 1990 if carried out without permission. The authorisation is what transforms the activity from criminal hacking to a legitimate security service.

Identifying Vulnerabilities: Ethical Hacking

ethical hacking is the broader discipline of which penetration testing is one technique. An ethical hacker (sometimes called a white-hat hacker) has the same knowledge and tools as a malicious attacker but operates within a legal and ethical framework agreed with the client. Ethical hacking may also include social engineering tests (e.g. attempting to trick staff into revealing passwords), physical security tests (e.g. trying to enter a server room without authorisation), and code review to find software vulnerabilities.

The value of ethical hacking is in perspective: an external expert approaching a system with fresh eyes, using attacker techniques, will find vulnerabilities that internal IT staff who designed the system might overlook. Many organisations engage ethical hackers before launching a new network, after a significant change, or on a regular schedule.

A school contracts a security firm to conduct a penetration test of its network before the start of term. The testers are given written authorisation from the headteacher. Over three days, they:

  • Scan all network devices for open ports and identify three devices running outdated software with known security flaws.
  • Attempt to connect a laptop to the school Wi-Fi using default router credentials — and succeed, because the admin password had never been changed.
  • Attempt to access the server room by following a member of staff through the door — this “tailgating” attempt succeeds because the door was propped open.

Their report details all three vulnerabilities with recommendations: update the outdated software, change the router’s admin credentials, and enforce a strict door-closing policy. The school fixes all three before term begins. Without the pen test, any of these vulnerabilities could have been exploited by a malicious attacker.

Protecting Networks: Access Control

access control is the first line of protection: ensuring that only authorised users and devices can connect to the network, and that each user can only access the resources appropriate to their role. In a school, a student account might have access to shared homework folders but not to the administration system. A teacher account has broader access. A network administrator has the highest level of access.

Access control is implemented through user accounts and passwords, combined with user permissions that define what each account can do. Strong access control requires regularly reviewing who has which permissions, disabling accounts when users leave the organisation, and ensuring that users do not share accounts or passwords.

Protecting Networks: Physical Security

physical security protects the hardware that a network runs on. No amount of software-based security matters if an attacker can walk into a server room and physically remove a hard drive. Physical security measures include:

  • Locked server rooms — restricting entry to authorised personnel only, often using key cards, PIN pads or biometric readers on doors.
  • Cable management — securing network cables so they cannot be easily unplugged or tampered with.
  • Locked equipment — physically securing network switches and routers so they cannot be removed or reset.
  • CCTV and visitor logs — monitoring who enters secure areas and maintaining a record that can be reviewed after a security incident.

Protecting Networks: Firewalls

A firewall acts as a gatekeeper between a trusted internal network and an untrusted external one — typically the internet. It examines each data packet and decides, based on rules set by the network administrator, whether to allow it through or block it. A school might configure its firewall to block traffic to certain categories of website, reject all incoming connections on ports not used by school systems, and alert the administrator when unusual patterns of traffic are detected.

Packet filtering is the most common firewall technique: the firewall inspects the header of each packet (looking at source IP address, destination IP address, port number and protocol) and either allows or blocks it based on the rules. A packet from an unknown external IP address trying to connect to an internal database server on a port that should not be publicly accessible will be blocked. A packet from a trusted address connecting on an expected port will be allowed through.

Key Fact

Three categories of network protection: Access control — user accounts, passwords and permissions ensure only authorised users can connect and limit what they can do. Physical security — locked server rooms, secured cabling and equipment prevent physical tampering. Firewalls — inspect and filter packets based on rules, blocking unauthorised traffic between the internal network and external networks such as the internet.

Identification and protection are complementary, not alternatives. Access control, physical security and firewalls reduce the chance of a successful attack. But no defence is perfect: new vulnerabilities appear constantly as software changes, new devices are added and human behaviour varies. Penetration testing and ethical hacking identify weaknesses that protections have missed or that have developed since protections were last reviewed. A mature security strategy uses both: robust protections, tested regularly by independent experts who try to break them.

Example: a firewall may block most unauthorised traffic, but a pen test might discover that a misconfigured rule allows traffic through on an unexpected port. Without the pen test, this misconfiguration might go unnoticed until a malicious attacker finds it first.
exam_tip_html: For network security questions, the specification organises answers around two categories: identifying vulnerabilities (penetration testing, ethical hacking) and protecting networks (access control, physical security, firewalls). Structuring your answer around these two categories helps ensure you cover the right material. For an Explain question, always pair a statement of what the method does with a reason why it improves security — stating “a firewall blocks packets” scores one mark; adding “which prevents unauthorised external traffic from reaching internal systems, reducing the risk of a successful attack” scores the second. Never confuse penetration testing with malicious hacking in an exam answer — always state that it is authorised.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Identifying vulnerabilities: penetration testing and ethical hacking are authorised techniques that use attacker methods to find weaknesses before malicious actors do. The Computer Misuse Act 1990 makes the same techniques criminal without explicit permission.
  • Protecting networks: access control (user accounts and permissions) restricts who can connect and what they can do; physical security (locked server rooms, secured hardware) prevents physical tampering; firewalls filter packets based on rules to block unauthorised traffic.
  • Identification and protection work together — protections reduce risk, and regular penetration testing finds the gaps that protections have missed.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes penetration testing?
A) Installing anti-malware software on all network devices
B) Monitoring network traffic to detect unusual patterns
C) Attempting to access a network without authorisation to expose vulnerabilities to malicious attackers
D) Attempting to gain access to a network with the organisation’s permission to identify security weaknesses
practice_questions.marks: D) Attempting to gain access to a network with the organisation’s permission to identify security weaknesses [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State one example of a physical security measure used to protect network infrastructure.
practice_questions.marks: Any one of: locked server room / key card or PIN access to server areas / CCTV in server rooms / cables secured and managed to prevent tampering / equipment physically locked to racks. [1 mark]

Mastering: A network security device that monitors incoming and outgoing network traffic and decides whether to allow or block specific packets based on a set of predefined security rules, acting as a gatekeeper between a trusted internal network and an untrusted external network.
Secure: Monitors/filters network traffic based on rules; prevents unauthorised access.
Developing: A device that blocks unwanted internet traffic.
Emerging: Something that protects the network (too vague). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how access control is used to protect a school network.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Access control requires users to log in with a unique username and password to connect to the network. User permissions restrict what each account can do: student accounts may only access shared folders and the internet, while teacher accounts can access mark books and assessment data, and administrator accounts can change network settings. This ensures that even if an attacker gains access to one low-privilege account, they cannot access sensitive system files or other users’ data.
Secure: User accounts and permissions described with a school-appropriate example of different access levels.
Developing: States that users need passwords to log in; does not explain permissions.
Emerging: Vague description of restricting access without mechanism. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between penetration testing and ethical hacking.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Penetration testing is a specific technique within the broader discipline of ethical hacking — it involves attempting to access a network or system without legitimate credentials to find vulnerabilities, with written authorisation from the organisation. Ethical hacking is the broader practice that includes penetration testing but also social engineering tests (e.g. attempting to trick staff into giving up passwords), physical security tests (e.g. trying to enter a server room without authorisation), and software code review. Both involve using attacker techniques with permission, distinguishing them from criminal hacking.
Secure: Penetration testing correctly defined as a specific technique; ethical hacking correctly identified as the broader discipline, with at least one additional technique named.
Developing: Both terms described but the relationship (pen test is a type of ethical hacking) not made clear.
Emerging: Both described vaguely; no meaningful distinction. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Discuss the effectiveness of firewalls and physical security as methods of protecting a network, identifying the limitations of each.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Firewalls — effective at filtering malicious packets from external networks, can block traffic on specific ports and IP ranges, and can alert administrators to suspicious activity. Limitation: firewalls do not protect against threats already inside the network (e.g. an attacker who gains legitimate credentials), and sophisticated attacks may use allowed ports to bypass rules. Physical security — essential because software protections are useless if hardware can be physically removed. Locked server rooms prevent direct tampering; cable management prevents physical interception. Limitation: physical security only protects on-site infrastructure and relies on human behaviour (e.g. not holding doors open for others); it cannot protect data in transit across external networks. Overall: both methods are necessary but neither is sufficient alone — a well-designed network uses multiple overlapping layers of protection.
Secure: Both methods discussed with a valid limitation each; some comparison or evaluative comment.
Developing: Both methods described with one limitation between them; limited evaluation.
Emerging: Only one method discussed meaningfully. [6 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: What makes penetration testing legal and ethical, rather than criminal?
options: Having explicit written authorisation from the organisation
Only testing your own personal devices

knowledge_checks.q: Which network protection method examines each data packet and decides whether to allow or block it based on a set of rules?
Access control restricts which _____ and devices can connect to a network and what they are permitted to do.
Locking server rooms and securing network equipment are examples of _____ security measures.
Match each network security method to its description:
right: Authorised attempts to break into a network to find vulnerabilities
User accounts and permissions that restrict who can connect and what they can do
Monitors and filters network traffic based on predefined security rules

flashcard_questions.a: Authorised attempts to access a network to find vulnerabilities before attackers do.

flashcard_questions.q: What law makes penetration testing without permission a criminal offence?
What is the difference between penetration testing and ethical hacking?
flashcard_questions.a: Ethical hacking is the broader discipline; pen testing is one specific technique within it.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the credential that a user account checks at login before granting network access.
What are user permissions in the context of network security?
flashcard_questions.a: Rules defining what actions a user account is allowed to perform on the network.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one example of a physical security measure for protecting network hardware.
flashcard_questions.a: A locked server room with key card or PIN access.
Monitors and filters network packets, blocking those that break its security rules.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the firewall technique that inspects each data packet against a set of allow/deny rules.
Why is physical security necessary even when software protections are in place?
flashcard_questions.a: Software cannot prevent an attacker who physically removes or tampers with hardware.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the two categories of network security methods in the specification.
flashcard_questions.a: Identifying vulnerabilities (pen testing, ethical hacking) and protecting networks.

glossary_terms.definition: The combination of processes, practices and technologies designed to protect a network, its infrastructure and the data it carries from unauthorised access, misuse or attack.

An authorised test in which security professionals attempt to gain access to a network or system without using legitimate credentials, in order to identify vulnerabilities before malicious attackers can exploit them.
The practice of using attacker techniques to find and expose vulnerabilities in a network or system, with explicit authorisation and the goal of improving security rather than causing harm.
A security mechanism that restricts which users and devices can connect to a network and what they are permitted to do, enforced through user accounts, passwords and permission levels.
The set of actions a user account is allowed to perform on a network or system, such as read, write, delete or execute, assigned by an administrator based on the user's role.
Measures that protect the physical infrastructure of a network from unauthorised physical access, including locked server rooms, cable management and secured equipment.
A network security device that monitors incoming and outgoing network traffic and decides whether to allow or block specific traffic based on a set of predefined security rules.
